questions.question: Define discharge and distinguish between slow and sudden discharge with an example of each. Explain how a spark forms and why an everyday static shock is usually harmless.
questions.expected_answer: Discharge is the loss of charge from a charged object (negative: extra electrons flow away; positive: electrons flow onto it). Slow discharge: charge leaks gradually, e.g. a balloon on a wall losing charge to humid air, or earthing through a wrist strap. Sudden discharge: a spark, e.g. a shock from a car door or lightning. When charge is large enough (about 30 000 V per cm of dry air), the few charged particles in the air are accelerated, knock electrons off molecules and create a conducting channel; charge rushes through, heating the air so it glows and cracks. A static shock is harmless because the amount of charge is tiny and it flows for a very short time, even though the voltage is high.

questions.question: Explain how a thundercloud becomes charged, how lightning occurs, and what causes thunder. Thunder is heard 6 s after a flash; estimate the distance.
questions.expected_answer: In a cumulonimbus cloud, rising and falling air makes small ice crystals collide with larger soft hail pellets; charge transfers, small crystals become positive and are carried to the top, heavier pellets become negative and collect lower, so the base becomes negative. The negative base induces a positive charge on the ground. When the charge is large enough, a stepped leader travels down through the air, a streamer rises from a tall object, they connect and a huge current (return stroke) flows, seen as the flash. The channel is heated to about 30 000 °C, so the air expands explosively, producing thunder. Sound travels about 1 km in 3 s, so 6 s ÷ 3 ≈ 2 km.

questions.question: Give four lightning safety rules with reasons, explain why a metal car is safe, and describe how a lightning conductor protects a building.
questions.expected_answer: Go indoors into a solid building when thunder is heard (if you can hear thunder you can be struck); do not shelter under a lone tree (tall objects are struck and current can jump to you); avoid open fields and hilltops (you may be the tallest object); avoid water, metal fences and washing lines (good conductors); wait about 30 minutes after the last thunder; indoors avoid baths and plugged-in appliances. A closed metal car body conducts the current around the outside to the ground (Faraday cage), not the tyres. A lightning conductor is a pointed metal rod on the highest point connected by a thick copper or aluminium strip to a plate buried in the ground; if lightning strikes, current flows safely through the conductor into the Earth instead of through the building.
